accuracy.evidence: The four target emotions and their cues follow the facial action descriptions used in FACS-based research: happy = lip corners raised with cheek raise (AU12+AU6), sad = inner brow raise with lip-corner depressor (AU1+AU15), angry = brows lowered and drawn together (AU4), scared = brows raised with wide eyes and open mouth (AU1+2+5+26). The lab's classifier feel(b,m) encodes exactly these rules, and a turned-down mouth with neutral brows is honestly labelled 'sad or angry?' rather than forced. The adult note on affect labelling reflects Lieberman et al. (2007), where naming a feeling reduced amygdala response. PSED goals match DfE Development Matters (talk about their feelings using words like happy, sad, angry or worried).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips young children and adults actually make: confusing sad with angry because both mouths turn down (Angry step predict, the 'Look at the eyebrows' challenge feedback, p3, m8); thinking a downturned mouth alone decides (new 'frown' state asks the child to move the eyebrows); believing there is one right feeling (stories with two accepted answers such as the tower falling: sad or angry, m6); and treating anger as a bad or grown-up-only feeling (the ok challenge tags bad and big, m2).

lab_distinct.evidence: No other lab builds a face: the child drags eyebrow and mouth handles on a large cartoon face whose expression and name update live, then drags feeling-word chips onto four animated stick children whose posture (slumped, stamping, jumping, shaking) carries the clue. The interaction model is expression shaping and body reading, unlike the sorting, plotting or counting labs elsewhere, and the distinctness gate passed against all registered labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step changes exactly one cue so the cause is visible: Happy moves only the mouth; Sad starts from a happy face so the child must both drop the mouth and lift the brows; Angry keeps the turned-down mouth and only the eyebrows change, which isolates the sad versus angry clue; Scared pushes brows high with a neutral mouth. Body clues extends the idea from faces to whole bodies, and the free 'Any face' step invites a grown-up to name the child's face, practising labelling both ways.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions are locked in before the child acts and are answered by what they then build: which way a happy mouth curves, which way sad eyebrows go, what distinguishes sad from angry (mouth, eyebrows, or cannot tell), and which feeling a slumped child shows. Each completion message restates the prediction and explains why the right option holds, via A.reveal, so wrong guesses are confronted with the face the child has just made.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles four kinds (read a face, a story, a body description, and 'is it OK to feel angry?') with rotated answer order. Feedback is specific to the wrong choice: picking sad for an angry face says pulled-down brows mean angry; picking happy for a frown says the mouth does not curve up; story mistakes name the better fits; 'angry is bad' gets 'it tells you something feels unfair; what you do next matters'. Stories with two valid feelings accept both and say people can feel different things.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation scores Flesch-Kincaid 1.2 and uses only short, concrete sentences about mouths, eyebrows and bodies; on-canvas text is single words (happy, sad or angry?) with large type. Adult text scores 5.9 and gives the action cues, the four common mistakes, and two concrete home routines (naming your own feeling with a reason, asking how a story character feels). Practice and mastery items use short child-scale stories with names and numbers.

no_filler.evidence: Every step has a job: three single-cue face builds, one combined scared face, a body-reading match, a free practice for parent-child play and a varied challenge. There is no decorative animation; the only motion is the stick figures' jumping and shaking, which are themselves the feeling clues, and it stops under reduced motion. Items each test a distinct cue or idea, from facial cues to why naming helps.

mobile.evidence: Verified on iPhone 13 and a 1200px desktop with real pointer drags: dragging the mouth and eyebrow handles changes the face and completes Sad; dragging each of the four chips onto the stick children completes Body clues. Handles have 24px-radius hit circles with a generous band across the whole face width, the lab opts into the young layout so answer buttons are at least 56px tall with larger text, and no page errors were logged in either viewport.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button route: Eyebrows up/down and Mouth up/down buttons, and per-child number buttons with labels like 'Put sad on child 1: shoulders drop, head hangs down, a tear'. The canvas aria-label and a polite live region describe the current face in words (eyebrows relaxed, mouth turned down) so the task works without sight. Feeling words are never shown by colour alone, and the axe check in the browser gate passed with no violations.
